In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying neuronal development in the retina.
the development of the human retina, in the first place, and with the differentiation processes in the retina, in the second place.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human retina is not only a model system for studying retinal development and differentiation, but also a model for the development of the central nervous system in general.
the retinal development in humans begins at 22 days of gestation.
the human retina is a complex structure with several different cell types.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the early human retinal development is similar to that of the mouse, with a few exceptions: the timing of the neurogenesis is faster in human; the number of progenitors is higher in human; the human progenitor cells are more proliferative and less prone to differentiation; the number of neurons is lower in human.
we have identified a novel population of cells in the human fetal retina that are not only capable of expressing neuronal markers, but also have the potential to differentiate into neurons.
the human retina develops from the optic cup, and the retinal progenitor cell (RPC) is the cell that produces the neurons and glial cells of the retina.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the early human retina is a dynamic environment with a large number of cells that undergo cell death.

the early retinal progenitors have a very limited ability to differentiate into neuronal cells and the main source of neurons is the progenitors that are generated in the later stages of the retinal neurogenesis.
the early human retinal progenitor cells (hRPCs) are multipotent and can be induced to differentiate into neurons, glial cells and photoreceptor cells.
